utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the usher turn on the microphone of the witness. Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lucic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd just like to suggest that this witness be advised of his rights under Rule 90(E). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lucic, before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Excellency. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel Lucic.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D6088 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, have you provided a statement to the Defence team and is that statement before you now?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have provided a statement and I can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am waiting for interpretation and I would kindly ask you to do the same so that we would have everything in the transcript. Does the statement accurately reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Basically everything is in it in the way I put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I was to ask you today in the courtroom the same questions, will your answers to those questions be the same in essence as they stand in the statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, in essence, although perhaps certain dates may vary up to between 10 and 15 days since I couldn't recall everything exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I seek to tender this statement under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it that you are also tendering three associated exhibits? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Is the Trial Chamber minded to admit those associated exhibits? If so, we can add them to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Actually, at the moment not. The Chamber is not satisfied that those three exhibits referred to in para 35 that do form an indispensable and inseparable part. So if the accused is minded to tender those documents, he should lead live with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we're not minded to tender those, so we'll withdraw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll give the number for the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6088 becomes Exhibit D2516, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't ask your opinion, but I take it you didn't object to the admission? Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wanted to read out a summary of Colonel Lucic's statement in the English language. [In English] Vlade Lucic is a retired colonel. After graduation from the military academy in 1975 he was posted to serve in Maribor, Slovenia, where he worked as an officer of the JNA. He was then transferred to Celje, Slovenia. After the secession of Slovenia from Yugoslavia in 1991, his unit, a motorised brigade, was relocated to Cacak in Serbia, where he worked until May 1992, when he received orders to report to the Sarajevo Corps and assigned to the 216th Mountain Brigade under the command of Colonel Dragomir Milosevic, who ordered him to take over the command of the infantry battalion. Colonel Milosevic drove him to Grbavica where they came under strong Muslim fire. This unit was made up mostly of troops from Sokolac, nearby municipality. He was the commander of the 2nd Battalion from May the 18th, 1992, until the end of January 1993. He immediately noticed that the lines were not covered with enough men, that the defence was not linked in, and that the establishment of weapons were missing. At that time, the JNA Marsal Tito barracks were under the blockade with JNA soldiers inside, cadets, and all the weapons in it. They had the task to lift the blockade if possible, but they could not do so because the Muslim forces kept their positions under continuous fire. On 22nd of May, 1992, the 1st Romanija -- Infantry Romanija Brigade was established. It was created from what was originally the 2nd Mountain Brigade. Only the title changed and everything else remained the same. After January 1993 he was moved to the command of this brigade to operation and training duties where he remained until the end of the war. The 1st Corps of the BH Army was in the parts of the city of Sarajevo which were under Muslim control during the period from April 1992 to 1995. During the entire war, Colonel Vlade Lucic's unit's line of defence was established at all -- was not established at all towards Gorazde across Mount Gosina, 50 kilometres in length. The strategy and objectives of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in relation to the city of Sarajevo was to prevent the penetration of the BH Army into the Serbian territory, as this would have been fatal for the Serbian population and its soldiers and would have had a huge impact on the development of the war situation in other fronts and on the course of the war in BH in general. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps mainly conducted defensive operations due to the lack of manpower, while the Muslim units were almost always on the offensive. His unit's offensive operations were mainly designed to recapture lost positions and to neutralise their weapons and manpower in locations from which they were engaging civilian and military targets on the Serb side. He and his unit were aware of the international conventions that protect the civilian population in the war, so they opened fire in self-defence and only against military targets, while the Muslim forces ceaselessly fired at civilians, especially those fleeing their terror in the city towards the Serbian territory. Soldiers in his unit who violated these legal norms were subjected to disciplinary action in case of mild breaches and to criminal sanctions in cases of severe breaches, but the necessary investigations were first conducted by persons authorised to do so by law. Vlade Lucic and his unit had knowledge that the VRS general headquarters and the civilian authorities of the Republika Srpska had extended offers to the city of Sarajevo to be fully demilitarised and that the heavy weapons be put under the control of the United Nations, but they didn't know that the ultimate objective of the Serbian authorities was to -- that the city of Sarajevo be split up, nor did they know about the initiative to put Sarajevo airport under the control of the UN in June 1992, but he believes that humanitarian reasons were behind this. They had -- the army, his own brigade had a pretty good intelligence and information about the zones of responsibility of the 1st Corps of BH Army, including the depth of the territory which also comprised civilian areas of the city under Muslim control, so they had knowledge that Muslims were using snipers from the tall buildings on the opposite side where civilians lived, as well as using mortars mounted on mobile off-road vehicles. They also had intelligence about the positions of the opposing forces in the dominant high spots in and around the city under the control of the Muslim forces, from where they targeted civilians and soldiers. This rendered Grbavica, Vrace, Lukavica, and other places no-go areas on the Serb side. Likewise, they had knowledge that the 1st Corps of the BH Army had a huge numerical advantage and was armed with all kinds of cutting-edge weapons and artillery and that they had large quantities of ammunition and shells. Muslim mortars targeted their positions -- Serb positions from the train station, from the tunnel in Ciglane settlement, from the grounds of the Kosevo Hospital, and from local -- other locations which were mostly civilian zones and civilian facilities. Because they knew that Muslims were misusing civilian buildings for military purposes, they had to -- they had that fact in mind when returning fire and took care not to endanger the lives of civilians in the territory of the opposing side. Vlade Lucic's unit had no intention of causing civilian casualties through fighting. It also did not have any intention of terrorising civilians who were under the control of the Muslim authorities. They never received any orders from the higher commands or civilian authorities to carry out attacks on the means of public transport. It was meticulously explained to his own soldiers and commands that military targets were and, especially, that civilians must not be attacked. They engaged the enemy only on orders and, if necessary, only in direct military objectives. Vlade Lucic filed reports to inform his superior command and the peacekeeping force located on the battle-field of Muslim attacks from civilian zones and called their attention to the fact that the opposing units were not choosing their victims and that in the most cases they killed civilians. As to the commanding officers in his unit, they were mostly reserve officers, that means persons with higher education who had graduated from the school for reserve officers while doing their mandatory military service in the JNA. They were also a very small number of professional officers in the JNA. Privates were mostly local people referenced to as people's army who were deployed mainly according to their military or professional specialities. His unit did not have volunteers from other countries in its ranks, but he heard that there were some in other units and that superior commands and civilian authorities had taken a negative stance in relation to them. During the period when he was the commander of his unit, he was the only professional officer and does not believe that the shortage of the professional personnel had a major impact on the quality of command because they conducted further training for the command personnel and worked on establishing professionalism in commanding, although of course it would have been better if the commanders had in fact been professional officers. They sometimes had problems in achieving effective control over the members of his unit which is normal but those problems were never ignored. Ammunition supply in his unit was solid or at a satisfactory level, yet still under strict control by command and commanding officers and therefore there was no ammunition misuse, least not in his unit. Within his unit there were snipers as per the unit establishment, and if they engaged targets they were only military targets so that civilians in the city under Muslim control did not come under sniper fire. On the contrary, Muslim snipers killed, especially in Grbavica, a very large number of civilians of different ethnic backgrounds, but mostly Serbs fleeing to Serbian territory. The general stance of the superior command of the VRS and of the civilian authorities of the Republika Srpska was not to prevent but rather to enable the humanitarian organisations to deliver humanitarian aid to the civilians under Muslim control. They ensured free and safe passage for humanitarian convoys through the territories under their control. Vlade Lucic's unit did not have specific knowledge that humanitarian convoys were misused for military purposes for the benefit of the 1st Corps of BH Army, but Muslim forces would intensify their operations using weapons they did not have until then, which may indicate that they were, in fact, misusing said convoys to obtain weapons. They also had no knowledge of the existence of a black market in which humanitarian aid goods were being sold in the territory under Muslim control. They did however learn from the media and fleeing Serbian citizens about the existence of criminal groups with the units of the BH Army 1st Corps terrorising the Serbian civilian population by imprisoning them in and in detention camps, levying unfounded accusations against them, raping them, and so on. They also repeatedly violated cease-fire agreements. Supreme Commands and civilian authorities took a liberal stance with regard to the freedom of movement of civilians toward the city and out of the city under Muslim control. On the contrary, it is a notorious fact that the Muslim authorities did not allow civilians to leave the territory under their own control. His unit and the civilian authorities of the municipality in which his unit's zone of responsibility was located co-operated well and did not have any problems. He is not aware of there being a Serbian municipal policy of persecution, murder, and discrimination based on ethnic, religious, or other differences. He also has no knowledge about the relationship of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps headquarter with republican civilian authorities or the president of the VRS. With regard to aerial bombs, modified aerial bombs, fuel air bombs, and other air-to-surface missiles, Vlade Lucic does not know that Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had or used in combat operations such bombs or missiles. And that would be it, a short summary, and I don't have any questions for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you introduced the witness as a retired colonel. Could you ask him when he retired from the army, until when he served in the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, when did you leave the army and when did you retire?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I retired in 2002. Following that I was a contracted officer in the VRS until 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that you had gone -- undergone all the checks carried out by international forces for all the personnel who were to serve in the armed forces after the war, or rather, did you undergo such checks?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I suppose as much. No one called me to perform any kind of particular checks, but given the fact that I was employed I believe I had undergone some checks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave I would like to offer Colonel Lucic a hard copy of his statement for perusal during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any problem. Show it to the Prosecution and hand it over to the witness. Mr. Lucic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief was mainly admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Prosecutor. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lucic.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have very limited time today so I would like to ask you to focus your answer as specifically as possible on the precise question that I ask. In your statement you explained how you served as the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Brigade up until the end of January 1993, and you described your area of responsibility as being from the Vrbanja bridge along the Miljacka river as far as the stadium, all areas within Grbavica. You also explained that you only commanded a part of the battalion, that's at paragraph 36 of your statement. And the Chamber has received evidence that 2nd Battalion units actually stretched along Ozrenska Street and in the direction of Lukavica. So my question for you is: Who commanded that part of the battalion, along Ozrenska Street and towards Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, in that part of Ozrenska Street facing Lukavica there was another unit that did not belong to my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: By "another unit," do you mean a unit that didn't belong to the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes. The area of responsibility is generally given to a brigade, whereas a battalion is a lower-ranking unit within a brigade. It just has its combat disposition. It does not have an area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So according to you what was the unit that was positioned along Ozrenska Street and towards Lukavica? What unit was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion was the unit deployed there, as far as I can remember, and it was mobilised in that area too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You also explained that when Dragomir Milosevic took you to the command in Grbavica in May 1992 you were ordered to take over from the Commander Beronja and that Beronja's deputy, Dragan Tupajic, remained your deputy commander. Had Beronja and Tupajic previously been officers in the 216th JNA Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: At the time Captain Beronja was a professional officer and he was deployed in the centre of military schools at the Marsal Tito barracks, whereas Dragan Tupajic was a civilian who had a different profession but at the same time he was a reserve officer. And his war time assignment was the 216th Brigade. Captain Beronja in peace time served in the barracks, but his war time assignment was also in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you said at paragraph 4 that the unit was made up mostly of troops from Sokolac. Were those troops also from the 216th Brigade previously?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And then you explained in your statement that around February of 1993 you moved to the command of the 1st Romanija Brigade to operations and training duties where you remained until the end of the war, and that's at paragraph 6 of your statement. Were you the assistant commander for operations and training? Was that your position in the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No. The brigade command is considerably bigger than battalion commands that are below it, and it has its professional services involved in different activities. I was in this department, if you will. At the time it was called the department for teaching and operations. It played no command role whatsoever. It is a professional organ and it was not part of the inner circle, if you will, of the command that comprised the commander, the deputy commander, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So what exactly were you duties? If you could briefly explain your duties when you were in the brigade command in this position in the teaching and operations department.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: For the most part, these were professional duties starting with organising work at the command post, then providing security for the command post; organising duty service, then also communication between duty officers who communicated with lower-ranking units, subordinate units all the time; then also checking on the professionalism of the units, carrying out training, and other tasks that were given to us by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. When you were within the brigade did you -- was it part of your duties to read and be familiar with orders that came to the brigade from the corps command?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, the orders that pertained to that department and that were sent to us by the commander, we read them and we acted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But if they were operational orders, that was something that would be outside of your area and you wouldn't necessarily have been familiar with those kinds of orders from the corps command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: For the most part we were aware of all orders because there was team-work involved. We were supposed to stand-in for each other too, but it wasn't necessary because there were orders that pertained to other professional organs in the command, but then we were not made aware of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you participate in meetings of the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how often were those meetings held?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the unit in 1992, these meetings took place very frequently, every day, because most of the personnel did not know one another. So - how should I put this? - they arrived in the unit ad hoc. The situation made it necessary, therefore, to have meetings every day until the brigade command was positioned in another location. At that point in time, meetings were not held every day any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 22 of your statement you said there were not very many professional officers, but you explained that you didn't believe that shortage - I'm referring to paragraph 22 - you didn't believe that the shortage of professional personnel had a major impact on the quality of command. At paragraph 23 you said you sometimes had problems in achieving effective control over members of the unit which is normal but the problems were not ignored. And you said it in example when a number of men abandoned the unit and causing you recruitment problems. My question is: Did you ever have an instance either when you were battalion commander or when you were a member of the brigade command whether any member of your units was suspected to be involved in any serious violations such as unlawfully targeting civilians? Do you recall any instance like that within your units?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: In my unit there were no cases of unlawful firing. Fire was only opened in necessary defence, but there were other crimes in the unit and appropriate measures were taken against the perpetrators of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you say "in my unit," are you referring to both the battalion and the brigade, in both cases you say there were no instances of unlawful firing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: When I speak of my unit I'm referring to the battalion, and I claim that there was no unlawful firing there. But at meetings I had never heard of any unit within the brigade opening fire unlawfully. But of course I cannot fully assert that because I was not present in all those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you never conducted any inquiries or initiated any investigations into any suspected instances of unlawful targeting of civilians I take it?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Well, if the question were to be raised in the brigade command as to whether someone had violated a cease-fire or opened fire unnecessarily, of course we would discuss that in our unit too and we would always reach the conclusion that no such thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how many times did that happen when a question was raised in the brigade command as to whether someone had violated a cease-fire or opened fire unnecessarily? How many times did that issue come up?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether a specific investigation was carried out with a view to a particular case, but at every meeting that was raised, that fire should not be opened, that that was prohibited, and that units should only protect themselves if attacked, that means self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But that's not exactly my question. My question was: How many times at the brigade command was there a specific issue of somebody opening fire unnecessarily? Did that -- did any specific instances ever get raised at the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I am not familiar with any such thing, that anyone had violated the rules for opening fire. So I'm not aware of any such thing, but it was on the agenda, namely, that fire should not be opened. Sometimes there would be a smaller attack launched against the unit and then the unit would respond and then the command would look into that, whether it was necessary to respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move on to another topic. At paragraph 17 of your statement you said that mortars targeted your positions from the train station, the tunnel, and the Ciglane settlement, the Kosevo Hospital, and other locations in civilian zones. And I understand from that that these -- this was when you were in the battalion command and they were targeting your positions in Grbavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And again at paragraph 19 you said that you had intelligence that behind the unit opposite you there were certain military targets such as heavy weapons and communications means, but you couldn't engage those targets because your unit was an infantry unit. Again, are you talking here about your battalion being an infantry unit?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes. My unit, the battalion, was an infantry unit, an infantry battalion with infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right. But even though it was an infantry unit, you still had smaller-calibre mortars, like 60-millimetre mortars; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And with a 60-millimetre mortar from Grbavica you could easily reach targets in the depth of Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Well, we didn't experiment in terms of what the range of the mortars was. The range is well-known. But basically they were there only to prevent attacks, that is to say penetration into Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. When you say "the range is well-known," the -- a 60-millimetre mortar could reach -- you could fire over 2 kilometres with a mortar like that; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: What, in your opinion, is the range of a 60-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: 60-millimetre mortar shell has a minimum range of 80- to 100 metres and they were not used. I mean, the purpose was just to prevent attacks in front of the company. They did not fire in-depth and also they did not fire unless they were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You've said that the minimum range is 80- to a hundred metres, but you didn't give a maximum range. I put to you that the maximum range of a 60-millimetre mortar is over 2 kilometres. Do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Well, that's possible theoretically, but in practice that was never carried out because what is needed there is - how should I put this? - fuses that regulate range.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 24065A, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, the document that is going to come up on your screen is a JNA fire tabling for an M57 60-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 13 in the B/C/S and page 11 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is the page with the ranges for the fourth charge, and you can see at the bottom of that page the maximum range is 2.538 metres for that charge; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24065A receives number P6015, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask that the witness be asked about the first line that has to do with fuses and could he say whether they had such fuses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a subject for you to take up in your re-examination, Mr. Karadzic. Let's continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lucic, you clearly then had weapons capable of firing back at these positions, such as the tunnel in Ciglane, the Kosevo Hospital, and other civilian areas from which you stated that you received fire in Grbavica. Is it your position that even though you were being fired at by mortars from these locations and you had weapons capable of reaching those firing positions, that you didn't fire back?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: As for information concerning from where they fired at our positions in Grbavica, we received that from our intelligence organs and observers too, but these were not the only locations from where fire was opened. However, we did not fire back. We did not respond to the fire that came from those locations because that was not our task.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript does not say: And our observers. So there's probably a difference between intelligence and observers because this belonged to their battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's there in the transcript: From our intelligence organs and observers too. Let's continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, you said -- just now you said that was not your task. Another Defence witness, a Mr. Izo Golic, has provided a statement to the Defence. He stated that he was in command of 120-millimetre mortar platoon within the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And his statement is at 1D06301.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And he stated that the 120-millimetre mortar battery was positioned at Ivanici and then at Petrovici and that they fired at positions in the city of Sarajevo from which the Muslim side fired on the battalion in Grbavica, and that can be found in paragraphs 16 and 18 of that statement. So based on what you've said about that not being your task, to fire into the depth of Sarajevo, and what Mr. Golic said in his statement, do I understand that you would communicate to other units within the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade when you received fire from the depth of the city and those units were responsible for returning fire at those locations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: My command in these cases communicated only with the superior command, with the brigade command, that is. The 120-millimetre battery was not within the battalion and it was not subordinated to the battalion either. It received its tasks also from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you would communicate to your brigade command when you were receiving fire from mortar positions in Sarajevo, and then the brigade command would issue instructions to the 120-millimetre mortar battery to return fire at those positions. Is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No. The brigade command was also at the location from which there was optical visibility in terms of this area. So when fire was opened that could be noticed without providing any kind of information. In such situations there was a duty officer who would provide information to some while we were at the positions there, at the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So in essence, however it was -- however the information was obtained, it was other elements of the 1st Romanija Brigade that was responsible for firing at positions inside -- in the depth of Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No, that is not my opinion. I don't know what fire they were responsible for and when they fired, because my position was in town on the Miljacka river, where visibility is 30 to 50 metres in front of the line, and then perhaps also 30 or 20 metres behind. All these units with 120-millimetre mortars were behind Vrace, the hill of Vrace. So it's not that there was any link between us. I mean, optical visibility or some other kind of link which would enable us to be in contact.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said: "I don't know what fire they were responsible for and when they fired ..." That's clear. When you were in the brigade command, you explained that you -- your duties were not operational. So is it correct then that you also were not involved in deciding what to fire on in the city and when with artillery or mortars?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No, I did not take part in that, but since the brigade command and the staff of the brigade are comprised of professional services as well, I was in the subordinate command, but I am not aware of any kind of selection of targets that was supposed to be engaged. Rather, targets from where fire was opened at our units were targeted. If there was a cease-fire, then not a single target was targeted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said at paragraph 12 of your statement that you knew that the VRS Main Staff and the civilian authorities of the RS had extended offers for the city of Sarajevo to be fully demilitarised and that heavy weapons be put under the control of the UN. Now, in fact, while the Bosnian Serb leadership did make such offers and in fact entered into agreements to that effect, they at the same time sought to undermine the effectiveness of these agreements by deceiving the UN monitors; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard about this. It was a sincere intention to remove the weapons with higher calibres from the area around Sarajevo to a further distance so that it would not be fired from those weapons onto the city. That was an order -- rather, not an order but the information we were aware of because the units needed to be prepared for a possible evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to look at P847, which is an order from the Main Staff precisely on that point, for preparation of a possible evacuation. This is a 9th of February, 1994, order from the Main Staff. And you can see at the beginning it says: "Due to the likelihood of reaching a cease-fire agreement around Sarajevo and in order to take urgent measures ..." The order is: "1. In the course of today and tomorrow the command of the SRK shell artillery from other positions towards Sarajevo, mainly inoperative weapons, which shall be put at the appropriate firing positions around Sarajevo." And then in the next paragraph it says: "If a cease-fire agreement for Sarajevo is signed these (inoperative) artillery pieces would again be removed from Sarajevo, while the current basic weapons would remain at the firing positions." And then further instruction is to bring in the inoperative weapons at night and pull them out if an agreement is reached only during the day and in good visibility to make it as evident as possible to - I think that should be - UNPROFOR and the Muslims. Now, this order in preparation for reaching a cease-fire agreement is aimed at deceiving the UN monitors by leaving inoperative -- removing inoperative weapons from the area and leaving the operative weapons in place; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this order. It is the first time I see it. As in 1994, the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade was not on the defence lines around Sarajevo, it was rather located in the Nisici plateau area with defence positions which were to prevent the Muslim forces from breaking through from the area of Zenica and Tuzla. These were the units of the 3rd and 4th Corps of the BH Army, and as for what was happening around Sarajevo I'm not aware of that. But I have never heard of this information, that there was an intention to deceive anyone. But the weapons that were supposed to be withdrawn were registered and then they were withdrawn indeed with UNPROFOR monitoring the process.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. On that note I'd like to look now at P1654, and this document is the agreement that was, in fact, reached, that the Main Staff had anticipated. And this document exists only in English, so I will read the operative parts to you. It's called "Points of Agreement." And it says that the following points were agreed at a meeting between Mr. Akashi and Dr. Karadzic. And under number 3 it says: "The establishment of a permanent armed UNPROFOR presence for control purposes ... at seven mutually agreed heavy weapons regrouping sites and at Lukavica Romanija Corps HQ. This is to be accomplished if possible by" midnight "19 February 1994 and no later than" midnight "on the 20th of February, 1994." And the agreement was entered on the 18th of February. And do you recall this agreement to regroup VRS weapons around Sarajevo into sites that could be monitored by the UN?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: My unit was at a distance of about 70 kilometres from Sarajevo at the time and its line of action was directed to the opposite direction from Sarajevo. There was not a single unit that was directed towards Sarajevo. And as for this information, this is something I see for the first time. However, I do know, thanks to the meetings, that it was ordered that the artillery weapons were to be grouped and placed under UNPROFOR monitoring, and I know that UNPROFOR made lists and checked all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You just said your unit was 70 kilometres from Sarajevo, but your unit had positions, among other places, at Hresa, which is in the near vicinity of Sarajevo, certainly within the 20-kilometre exclusion zone; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, the brigade did have positions facing Sarajevo up until 1994, and then the units, that is to say the battalions, were transferred. Some battalions remained there but they were now part of the composition of other units. When the command of the brigade moved to the Nisici plateau and the battalions which remained were resubordinated, so the command over them was taken over by the command which also remained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look now at 65 ter 23963. This is an SRK list dated the 21st of February, 1994. So this is one day after the dead-line for moving heavy weapons to the agreed monitoring sites had passed from the document we just looked at, and it is titled: "List of technical and material equipment that was not pulled out." And you can see there is a list for each of the brigades, and if we go to page 2 of the English, for the 1st Romanija Brigade it refers to a number of heavy weapons, including a series of weapons that are listed to be in Hresa and hidden in 3rd Infantry Battalion houses and similarly other weapons hidden in 4th Infantry Battalion houses. Now, these references to weapons that are not pulled out, including weapons that are hidden, in a report or a list issued the day after the dead-line expired for the weapons to be regrouped to monitoring sites reflects SRK efforts and 1st Romanija Brigade efforts to avoid implementing this exclusion zone agreement; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this list. As I already noted, when I moved to the brigade in 1993 I was mostly focused on organising defence towards Gorazde and Nisici plateau. So this was the outer ring directed in the opposite direction from Sarajevo. So I'm not aware of these battalions, the 3rd and the 4th. As far as I know, they were composed of the local population which did not move from those positions. And the units which left for the Nisici plateau, these were the battalions also formed on the territorial principle but in depth, as, for example, the Jahorina or Sokolac battalions and so on. And I am not aware of any orders like these or that anyone hid anything. I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we object because although it contradicts the testimony of the witness in some way, it's also not something that he would necessarily know about. So it's not directly impeaching and therefore wouldn't be admissible with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, it -- I disagree entirely. It impeaches the witness on a number of aspects, including the assertion that -- which seemed to shift over time, that the brigade was 70 kilometres away from Sarajevo as well as the denial that there were any efforts to deceive UN monitors. I think it's a direct impeachment and completely admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Ms. Gustafson and will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 23963 becomes Exhibit P6016, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at paragraph 24 of your statement, Mr. Lucic, you said that ammunition was under strict control of the command and there was no ammunition misuse, at least not in your unit. Were you aware of any ammunition misuse by the brigade when you were at the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of anything like that. The ammunition was used strictly in a professional manner. There were professionals on duty who had to register the consumption and supply with specific sorts of ammunition in the units. But at the meetings in the brigade, one of the items was always under logistics that there was not a sufficient amount of ammunition and that we really needed to economise with it so that we would not find ourselves in a situation that the unit cannot be supplied with ammunition and an attack might occur. So the unit commanders always made sure that they would have a reserve that would not be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you recall hearing anything at the brigade command about the fact that vast quantities of ammunition were being spent firing at inhabited settlements where there were no combat actions whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No, at the brigade command I did not hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that would constitute not only ammunition misuse, but unlawful activity, wouldn't it, if you were firing vast quantities of ammunition at inhabited settlements where there were no combat actions whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would be unlawful and unacceptable and it did not happen in my unit. And as far as I know, it also did not happen in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P2668, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, this is a 19 July 1995 warning from the SRK to brigades including the 1st Romanija Brigade. And if you look at the -- it's a warning about the rational expenditure of artillery ammunition and in the second paragraph it says: In spite of problems in ammunition production we very often fire at inhabited settlements and specific buildings when there are no combat actions whatsoever, spending vast quantities of ammunition ... And next paragraph it says: "It is inexplicable that some brigades spend much less ammunition in repelling three or more fierce attacks during the day than others that fire at inhabited settlements when there are no combat actions." Now I take it from your earlier answers that even though this warning was sent to your brigade, you didn't see it and you don't recall any discussion at the brigade about it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I have no seen this order and this has to do with artillery units so that I am not aware of it. But at the time when this order was written in 1995, I wish to inform you again that my unit, the 1st Romanija Brigade, was not facing Sarajevo. Its line of defence did not include any populated places. These were mountains and meadows and so on facing away from Sarajevo, but it's possible that this relates to some other units. In 1995 the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade did not have any artillery directed towards the 1st Corps positions in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lucic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, given the timing shall we take a break now? Yes. We'll break for 25 minutes and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. I'd just like to raise a very quick housekeeping matter with respect to one exhibit. We noted that a page is missing from P794, it's the last page, and we know that was an inadvertent omission because that particular page was explicitly referenced and quoted during the testimony of that witness. So I spoke with Mr. Robinson about it. We agreed that the simplest expedient is simply to add the page that was omitted, so if the Registry could unlock that, we can add the appropriate page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I see no problem. While we are dealing with this, Mr. Robinson, Friday, 30th November, the Prosecution filed its motion to exclude the evidence in part of witness Milan Pejic. And the witness is the fifth witness scheduled for this week. Also yesterday I noted an amended version has been filed. So could the accused be -- could be kind enough to respond to the motion by the end of close of business today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's already been filed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. Yes, Ms. Gustafson, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, at paragraph 33 of your statement you said you were not aware of there being a municipal policy of persecution in the zone of responsibility of your unit. But when you were based in Grbavica as a battalion commander there were large numbers of non-Serbs being expelled from Grbavica into the city; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No. Firstly, my unit did not have a zone of responsibility. Higher position, larger units had that. It only had a defence line which did not cover any territory, but just the shelters from which defence was conducted and I'm not aware that there were any expulsions -- not that I wasn't aware, but there weren't any expulsions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you've just said that you didn't have a zone of responsibility, but your statement says that you're not aware of a policy of persecution within the zone of responsibility of my unit, that's at paragraph 33. But your -- it's clear from your evidence you were based in Grbavica. If several hundred Muslims had been expelled in a single day in Grbavica, is that something you would have been aware of?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: The zone of responsibility here refers to my superior unit, and as for expulsions I never heard that there was any -- that there were any expulsions on such a large scale throughout the time I spent in Grbavica or in general. I mean, there was a general freedom of movement for civilians and my unit did not have any authority as regards the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to Exhibit P1266. The document you're about to see, Mr. Lucic, is a UN report from the 30th of September, 1992. And the report is titled: "Expulsion of Muslim Citizens From Grbavica ..." and in the first paragraph the drafter of the report explains that Mr. Abdelrazek of the UN requested this UN police unit to attend the Bristol Hotel. And in the fourth paragraph the drafter describes what happened. It says that there was a crowd of approximately 25 people and then an additional 50 people waiting to leave the area. There was shelling and gun-fire could be heard and the people were in a panic. And then it says that the writer was able to confirm that approximately 300 Muslim civilians have been expelled by the Serbs during the day from the area of Grbavica. It says 150 of them were gathered at the Bristol Hotel with the remainder at the Assembly building. And on the next page of the English, I see we've already gone to the next page of the B/C/S, it says that the Muslims travelled to the area by foot and used two different bridges, Vrbanja Most and the other one just behind the Bristol Hotel. And if we go down to the second-last paragraph, which would be on the next page of the B/C/S, it says that the writer found it very strange that this specific area of the town was under shelling. Based on the information and observations it appeared evident that the shelling was directed towards the Muslim civilians; all of them were confined in a specific area and the Serbians were well aware of that. And in the last paragraph the writer explains that they were later able to establish that the total number of people expelled during the day was between 500 and 700 persons. Now, as you've made clear in your evidence, you were stationed in Grbavica at the time as a battalion commander. Are you saying you were not aware of this event where 500 to 700 Muslim civilians were expelled by foot from Grbavica to the other side of the river?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, it is not quite clear to me. You have mentioned the Bristol Hotel and they were gathering there. Was it in order to cross or why did they gather at or near the Bristol Hotel? I -- this is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the report states that they had been expelled to the Bristol Hotel, and my question was whether you were unaware of the fact that in the area where you were stationed as battalion commander, that 500 to 700 Muslim civilians had been expelled from Grbavica in a single day?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of this, not at all, that there were any expulsions. I am aware that there were individuals who crossed over to the other side, but I don't remember when UNPROFOR came to Grbavica. Specifically, we did not have anything to do with civilians, regardless of the ethnicity. The soldiers had a defence line at Miljacka and shelters. They would stay in shelters. And when there was troop relief, then they would be in basements as shelters, and when they were relieved they would go to their homes. So I don't know what went on in the settlements. There were civilian authorities there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So did you ever hear about Batko or the nickname for Veselin Vlahovic who was committing crimes against non-Serbs in Grbavica? Did you -- were you aware of his activities at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No, I have not heard of this Batko.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 18392.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a report from the Vrace reserve police station of the 31st of May, 1992, and if we could go to page 2 of the English and stay on the same page in the B/C/S. And this is the second-last paragraph in the B/C/S and about the middle of the page in the English. And the police are explaining that there are some people in the territorial jurisdiction of our station undertaking operations on their own without any authority. They're carrying out searches. They're armed and in uniform, taking private and socially owned property, securities, and gold coins. And it says they blackmailed some people into giving them foreign currency to avoid being slaughtered or expelled. And it says foremost among them are members of the military police formed as part of the Novo Sarajevo Battalion, and it lists the names including Veselin Vlahovic whose nickname the Chamber has received evidence of was Batko. So this is a report from the Novo Sarajevo area at the time where you were operating as a battalion commander there. Is this also something you were not aware of, that this group was operating as members of the military police in uniform committing these crimes?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of this, but at meetings held at the command I said that they were held on a daily basis. There were warnings that in certain units any crime ought to be prohibited, or rather, prevented, prevented any sort of criminal offences, and in this period, that is to say between the 20th of May and in the next two months, there were 17 criminal proceedings in our units that the professional organs were in charge of because of a variety of crimes. But as for these groups who disguised themselves as units, I haven't heard of them. There was a military police unit in the brigade and in addition to the civilian police they also carried out their tasks. I'm not aware of what they were doing because this is the sort of information, data, that I had no access to and the same goes for this specific Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You just said there were 17 criminal proceedings in your units. What were those proceedings for, what crimes?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Those activities were not undertaken in my unit, but when there was a meeting in the command, when the security organ briefed all those present, the offences included theft, assaults on military personnel or civilians, attempted murders, and a number of other criminal offences that have prescribed sentence by law.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So that was -- you said that you heard about that at a meeting in the command and that briefing by a security organ. Was that security organ of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: It was the brigade security organ. The crimes had to do with the soldiers, members of the brigade. We did not have any information about civilians involved in criminal offences and what the police was doing. I have no idea exactly what the percentage was in the total number of offences pertaining to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go to page 3 in English of this document and page 2 in the B/C/S. At paragraph 28 of your statement you said civilians were given full freedom of movement to go in and out of the city, and I'd like to show you the last part of this document where it says from the aspect of intelligence it may be said that on the first line of combat and in the interior controlled by our forces, there were occurrences of persons crossing the first line of combat uncontrolled. And they give the example of Olga Mijacic who works as a nurse in the former military hospital and goes to and from work as do others who have close relatives in the Green Berets and over whom control should be established. Now contrary to your evidence about full freedom of movement, this document shows that the Novo Sarajevo authorities are controlling the movement of civilians in and out of the city; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see in the document, this was not about controlling the movement of civilians, but controls, checks. A vehicle is mentioned and it was checked whether the person driving the vehicle was indeed the owner or whether he stole it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, I think you might be looking at the wrong part of the document. I'm talking about the last paragraph where they talk about the problem of uncontrolled movement of persons across the line of combat, giving the example of a nurse named Olga Mijacic who goes to and from work. And her -- it says her -- in relation to her and others that control should be established. That's the passage I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I don't know where the nurse in question lived and in which hospital she worked. In any case, my unit did not control any civilian movement. Those who came over the bridge and over the Miljacka river and those going to the other side, we had no competence whatsoever. Of course under such restricted visibility circumstances, the soldiers had to monitor in order to prevent any military intrusion if there were people belonging to the military trying to cross over the river; otherwise, it was only the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Olga Mijacic, that would be a Serb name; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: She could be a Serb, a Croat. Olga could also be a Russian. I'd rather not draw any conclusions about her ethnicity based on her first name. She may be a Montenegrin as well, particularly if we look at the last name, Mijacic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 18395 receives number P6017, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, at paragraph 30 of your statement you talked about air bombs and modified air bombs and you said that you didn't know that the SRK had or used in combat such bombs or missiles. And I just want to get your position on that clear. Are you saying that the SRK didn't -- did not have or use any of these weapons, or are you saying that the SRK may have had and used these weapons but you personally don't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: The corps, as per establishment, does not have such weapons. As a rule, such weapons belonged to the air force. In any case, I have no knowledge of the corps having them or using them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if your brigade, the 1st Romanija Brigade, had air bombs, is that something that you would have been aware of, given your membership in the brigade command and your participation in their meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I don't know if the brigade had them and I don't know where they were stored and how many. These were not establishment assets and we had no plans at the unit level to use them under any circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So given that they're not establishment assets, if you did, in fact, have them at the brigade is that something that would be important enough to be discussed at the brigade meetings do you think?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'll try again. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You just said that air bombs were not establishment assets. So my question is if your brigade did obtain air bombs, given that they're not establishment weapons, would that have been something that would likely to have been discussed at the brigade command, at the meetings you attended?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: We wouldn't discuss it because these were not establishment assets. For routine supply, the brigade could not have received such weapons. Perhaps warehouses are a different issue because there were different things there from units which had withdrawn from Slovenia and Croatia. But air bombs is ammunition and you need a means, a vehicle, which is the plane. We didn't have that, it had not been planned and we did not have it available. There was no need for the brigade to have it because it had its own establishment assets. The weapons we had sufficed to implement the tasks we had received.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So to be clear, is it your position that the 1st Romanija Brigade did not have any air bombs?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: The 1st Romanija Corps [as interpreted] did not have such assets, air bombs. As for the warehouses and logistics, that is not something I'd be aware of in terms of what kind and quantities of ammunitions may there have been in the warehouses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the witness said Romanija Brigade, not Corps. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could look at P12 -- sorry, P1300, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, this is an order from the SRK to brigades including the 1st Romanija Brigade dated the 11th of July, 1995, and it orders units to issue air bombs to Major Simic on the 12th of July and specifically instructs the 1st Romanija Brigade to issue a 250-kilogramme air bomb to Major Simic. And if we could also look at P1315. This is another order from the SRK to brigades, including the 1st Romanija Brigade. This one's dated the 27th of August, 1995, and it explains that on orders of the Main Staff we are obliged to return air bombs from the Pretis factory from which they were pulled out, and it says that the units in the north-west section of Sarajevo return the air bombs as follows. And the 1st Romanija Brigade is instructed to return 205-kilogramme [sic] air bombs and two 250-kilogramme air bombs to the Pretis factory. And it's clear from these documents that your brigade, in fact, had multiple air bombs; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, if I understood this properly, Pretis was a civilian factory and as far as I can see the bombs were there and then were taken out due to the possibility of an attack. As for Major Simic who was mentioned in the first document, he was not a member of the 1st Romanija Brigade and I didn't know him at the time. As regards the take-over of air bombs and their return, I was not privy to that because I was in the operational part. I was focused towards the defence lines or working with the defence lines, whereas these are purely logistical matters. I was not involved in any transport of bombs. There is a lot of gunpowder, a lot of explosive material in the bomb and it is dangerous even to the person who possesses it. By using such bombs effects multiply and for security reasons it is unsafe for any units to be in the possession of such a bomb. In any case, I am not familiar with this and I am unaware of any information concerning the bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said these were purely logistical matters and you were in the operational part. In terms of the operational aspects of air bombs, your brigade was constructing an air bomb launcher, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that. The brigade had neither possibility nor capacity to create and mount such a launcher. The brigade consisted of soldiers, officers, and their personal weapons as well as the unit weapons. That was it. I don't know whether anything of this kind was made, and if it was it should have been put together in a plant somewhere where they had the means to produce it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P1285.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a request from the SRK command, again going to the brigades, including the 1st Romanija Brigade, requesting information by the 13th of June, 1995, including information on the number of aerial bomb launchers. And if we could now go to P1297. And this is the response from your brigade command to the SRK command saying that: "We do not have an air-bomb launcher (one is currently being manufactured)." Now, that's right that your brigade was manufacturing an air bomb launcher as this document states; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Well, no. As far as I can see, the document was signed by Major Branimir Curkovic. He was assistant commander for logistics. He was in charge of supplies for the brigade in terms of materiel and equipment, which he received from civilian structures and through military supply lines. I have no idea where he could have manufactured this, but in any case the launcher was not manufactured in the brigade. As for the rest of the items, it is only the 23-millimetre aircraft gun, which we call anti-aircraft gun, could also be used to target ground targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier you said that you -- as you said you participated in daily meetings of the brigade and you said that for the most part you were familiar with orders coming from the corps command to the brigade. And we've seen now a number of communications back and forth between the command and your brigade about the existence of air bombs, the fact that brigades had them, and the existence of air bomb launchers. Now, this is all going on at a time when you were a member of the brigade command. You must have known, even if you weren't personally involved, that the SRK had air bombs and air bomb launchers; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about this. Since the operational part was not situated close to the command, it was closer to the units engaged in defence. As for orders like this one - and I see that this was a coded telegram from the communications centre, such documents were taken by the officer to the commander, who then sent it directly to the officer responsible. In this case it would be the assistant commander for logistics. And it seems that this was communication between the assistant commander for logistics and the command. Such documents as this one were not received by other command organs. At the time in question, I was a desk officer in charge of education and training. We gave way to such officers who were familiar with the field and we had a reserve officer in the field who was familiar with the terrain. That is why I did not attend each and every meeting. This was not discussed by the command in its full composition, but this was strictly communication between the commander and the officer responsible for that particular area of activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move on to another issue that you address in your statement. At paragraph 26 you said that you knew that the general stance of your superior commands and the civilian authorities was not to prevent but rather to enable humanitarian organisations to deliver aid to the city. The Chamber has received evidence that in February of 1994 the UN brokered an agreement to create blue routes which allowed for humanitarian aid to be delivered across the airport into the city. And I refer to Harland's evidence at P820, paragraphs 89 to 90. Are you aware of this agreement on the creation of the blue routes?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: In general, I am familiar with that. I'm not familiar with the contents of the agreement, but I did know that there were routes that were to be used for the supply of humanitarian aid. I was also familiar with the command position that it should not be restricted in any way and that we were obliged to assist UNPROFOR if such assistance was requested.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But the airport was not in your brigade's area of responsibility; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: It was not in our area of responsibility at any time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So if there was an order to close the blue route across the airport, you wouldn't -- your brigade wouldn't have had anything to do with implementing that order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: It wouldn't, but such order never arrived and I don't know of any other units receiving such orders. In Sarajevo, for example, from my unit at least 50 per cent of all brigade unit members had relatives in that area who remained in Sarajevo and it was in their interest to have the aid reach the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P1639, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 23rd of July, 1994, from the Main Staff to the SRK commander, and it orders the SRK command to carry out all necessary preparations for the closure of the blue road, which goes across the airport, in order to prevent the transit of the Muslims as well as to prevent members of UNPROFOR and other humanitarian organisations from getting across the Sarajevo airport and going towards Igman and Lukavica and vice versa. Now, I take it this is an order that you were not aware of, given your answers to my earlier questions?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of this order. In any case, these are just preparations. As for any passage across the airport, it was used by the units at Bjelasnica and Jahorina. I wasn't aware of this order and I don't see whether it was implemented or not. I only see that preparations are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to P879. And page 3 of this document. This is a Main Staff report, and in the middle of the page under heading "II - Situation in the Territory," the second -- the second sentence says: "Due to sniper fire and the death of two girls, any movement of humanitarian organisations and convoys is prohibited until further notice." Is this another instance of you not being aware of orders or activities relating to humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: This document, I suppose if the general -- if the General Staff -- well, I didn't see it at the top who sent the document and who was supposed to receive it, in any case this was three levels above my command. I didn't see this order. In any case, it is stated that convoys should not be prevented from passing through.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I believe it states the opposite but I'll move on. You talked about snipers in your statement and you said that in your unit there were snipers, as per the unit establishment, but if they engaged targets these were only military targets. And when you were a battalion commander operating in Grbavica there were SRK snipers positioned in the tall buildings near the river; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. At our positions the soldiers were in combat groups of between five and ten in immediate physical vicinity, and the soldier who had been issued with a sniper was one of the group. Such people were not professional snipers but mobilised soldiers who were issued with sniper rifles. In the unit, in any case, were very few of them, perhaps one per company. Due to very short distances, commanders liked to exchange sniper rifles for automatic rifles which were way more efficient in case of close attack since the lines were only between 30 and 50 metres apart. A sniper rifle is not as useful as an automatic weapon if there is a group of enemy soldiers attacking you from relatively close by.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Just to be clear on your answer, you had snipers, you said you had soldiers issued with sniper rifle, and my question to you was that their positions -- do you deny that they were positioned in buildings in Grbavica close to the river?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes -- no, they were positioned within the unit; that is to say, shelters that had been dug out on the river-banks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to go now to P1060 which is an UNPROFOR document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, your time was up, but how much longer would you need to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm nearly done, Your Honours. I think less than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a protest from the UNPROFOR command to General Galic and it's dated the 18th of February, 1993. And this is just about the time that you left your position as battalion commander and moved to the brigade. And it says that on 15 and 16 February the location of the Ukrainian Battalion was exposed to sniper fire from Grbavica and it was determined that the sniper fire was coming from tall buildings near the river-bank. Did you hear about this incident, that General Galic was -- received a complaint about when you were either at the battalion command or at the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I had not heard of that because I had left. I think seven days before that I left Grbavica, but in my view this document is quite arbitrary. First of all, from the barracks you cannot see skyscrapers at Grbavica. But these tall buildings that are on the other side of the Miljacka, like Elektroprivreda and other buildings that are in the view if you look at Grbavica --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the answer. Could the witness please approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, the interpreters were not able to hear part of your answer because you seem to be answering a bit far from the microphone. Could you come closer to the microphone and repeat your last part of your answer which starts from the -- relate to -- which is related to Miljacka, like Elektroprivreda.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Grbavica, across the Miljacka river, towards the barracks, there are quite a few tall buildings that practically block these buildings at Grbavica. I did not climb up on these buildings, but I think that from Grbavica you cannot target the barracks because the barracks is the lowest facility surrounded by tall buildings in that part of town near the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you a portion of a video that's been admitted into evidence which is P806. There's no sound on the video so I'd just like you to watch the images on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We can stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This -- just for the record, this is between 1 minute, 58 seconds, and 2 minutes and 15 seconds of Exhibit P806. And this is a video that was taken when a journalist who was also a witness in this case, Mr. Van Lynden, visited a sniper position in an apartment block in Grbavica very close to the Miljacka river in September of 1992. And I refer to his evidence at P926, paragraphs 94 to 101. And contrary to your evidence a few moments ago that you did not have snipers near the river in buildings but that they were in shelters dug out on the river-banks, it's clear from this video that, in fact, you -- the SRK had snipers positioned in buildings in Grbavica; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I cannot conclude where this footage was taken as I look at it. You cannot see the location. You can only see it indoors here. I have my reservations. With regard to this, possibly it was not even taken in Grbavica; I cannot see that it is Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to now go to P1644 and page 2 of the English and page 1 of the B/C/S. If we could -- I'm told we need to switch from Sanction, whatever that means. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
